claim: The KOSPI [South Korea's stock index] had gone up almost 200% in the last 12 months [as of ~3 weeks before this video, i.e. its June 2026 peak], making South Korea the best-performing major stock market in the world
quote: gone up almost 200% in the last 12 months
evidence: KOSPI hit an all-time high of 9,385.59 on 19 Jun 2026, up ~100% YTD as of 3 Jun 2026 per CNBC/Goldman. Mid-2025 levels were in the ~3,000-3,200 range (banks 'eyeing a 3,200 breakout', Korea Herald, mid-2025). (9,385.59-3,200)/3,200 ~= +193%; (9,385.59-3,000)/3,000 ~= +213%. Either base puts the trailing-12-month gain to the June peak close to 'almost 200%'. Today's trailing-12-month figure (~115%, after the post-peak crash) is a different, lower number for a different date — this claim is about the pre-crash peak, which 'at one point... 3 weeks ago' supports.

claim: The S&P 500 [the main US stock index] only made [about] 24% [over the same 12-month period, for comparison]
quote: S&P 500, which only made 24%
evidence: Searched S&P 500 12-month and YTD return figures for mid-2026 three ways (direct query, FRED series, aggregator roundups); none of the results surfaced a synthesized number for this specific trailing window, only raw series pages. Directionally plausible given US equities were up double digits over the same period, but the 24% figure could not be pinned to a source.

claim: [At its 2026 peak,] Samsung was up over 500% at one point this year
quote: Samsung, was up over 500%
evidence: Samsung's 52-week range was KRW 67,500 (low) to KRW 374,500 (high): trough-to-peak = (374,500-67,500)/67,500 ~= +455%. Measured from the 2026 calendar-year open (~KRW 120,000, TradingKey) to the June peak, the gain was ~208-212%. Neither basis reaches 'over 500%' — the most generous available reading (~455%, and that trough wasn't even within 2026) falls ~45+ points short. Kernel of truth: a huge, real rally; the specific figure is inflated.

claim: [At its 2026 peak,] SK Hynix was up over 1,000% at one point this year, basically a 10x
quote: SK Hynix was up over 1,000%
evidence: SK Hynix's 52-week range was KRW 255,000 (low) to KRW 2,987,000 (high, reached 25 Jun 2026): trough-to-peak = (2,987,000-255,000)/255,000 ~= +1,071%. A separate tracker put its 1-year change at +1,125.59%. Both clear 'over 1,000%'.

claim: The top 10 companies in the S&P 500 [via ETFs like VOO] represent 36% of the index
quote: the top 10 companies represent 36% of this index
evidence: As of April 2026 the S&P 500 top-10 weight was reported at 35.59%, essentially matching '36%'. (Other 2026 readings range 33.8%-40.8% depending on exact date/methodology, so the figure moves around but 36% sits inside the documented range.)

claim: Samsung and SK Hynix together represent over 56% of the whole KOSPI [South Korea's stock market]
quote: represent over 56% of their whole stock market
evidence: Reported combined KOSPI weight for the two stocks: 51.5% (13 May 2026), 54.76% (mid-June), 60% (30 June 2026). 'Over 56%' sits inside that documented run-up.

claim: Roughly 14 million retail investors [in South Korea] put their savings and a huge amount of borrowed money into Samsung and SK Hynix stock
quote: that's roughly 14 million retail investors
evidence: Korean retail stock ownership is reported at 14-14.5 million people by end of 2025/2026 (up from ~6 million in 2019), with leveraged funds heavily concentrated in Samsung and SK Hynix. Matches.

claim: In just 21 days [in mid-to-late June/July 2026], the KOSPI dropped 25%
quote: in just 21 days ... The KOSPI dropped 25%
evidence: Multiple outlets report the KOSPI fell ~25% from its 19 June 2026 peak by mid-July (one puts it at 25% by 16 July, ~27 days; another headline states '25% in 3 weeks' verbatim). Close enough on both magnitude and window that minor day-count variance doesn't change the verdict.

claim: 1.2 million [Korean brokerage] accounts, which works out to be one in every 30 people in the country, got hit with margin call thresholds
quote: 1.2 million accounts, which works out to be one in every 30 people in the country
evidence: Reporting puts leveraged retail accounts hitting margin-call thresholds at 1.2 million, independently described elsewhere as 'one in every 30 adults in South Korea' facing liquidation risk — a near-verbatim match to the claim's ratio.

claim: Over 3 trillion won in investments were liquidated [forced-sold by brokers during the crash]
quote: over 3 trillion won in investments were liquidated
evidence: One source states forced liquidations reached 2.3 trillion won by 14 July (a running, growing total); another (matching the video almost verbatim) reports 'over 3 trillion won in stock' liquidated, consistent with the total continuing to climb over the following days.

claim: 320,000 [Korean brokerage] accounts were wiped out, some of them overnight
quote: 320,000 accounts were just wiped out, some of them overnight
evidence: Headline and body match closely: '320,000 Retail Accounts Wiped Out Overnight' during the KOSPI plunge.

claim: The president of South Korea held an emergency intervention for the stock market
quote: the president of South Korea held an emergency intervention for their stock market
evidence: Headline: 'President Steps In for Emergency Intervention' after forced liquidations and a bear-market plunge. Matches.

claim: South Korea has about 51 million people
quote: there's about 51 million people
evidence: South Korea's 2026 mid-year population is estimated at 51,600,388 (Worldometer, UN-derived). Matches.

claim: 14 million [South Korean] retail investors are one in four [Koreans]
quote: 14 million of them, or one in four, are what's called retail investors
evidence: Reporting states the ~14 million individual investors in listed companies equal 'about a quarter of the total population' against South Korea's ~51-51.6 million people — matches the stated ratio directly.

claim: A [unnamed] Korean investor featured in a documentary had a portfolio worth over $650,000, was up 150%, and her biggest holdings were leveraged ETFs — she wouldn't show her face on camera because her family didn't know how much leverage she was using
quote: Her portfolio was worth over $650,000, and she was up 150%
evidence: An anonymous individual's personal portfolio in an unnamed documentary — no named subject or source to check against.

claim: At the peak, Koreans invested about 10 trillion won into leveraged funds betting on just one company
quote: Koreans invested about 10 trillion won into leveraged funds betting on just one company
evidence: Reporting on Korea's single-stock leveraged ETFs (launched May 2026, tracking Samsung and SK Hynix separately) puts combined peak AUM across both stocks at ~17 trillion won, with 14-15 trillion won in net inflows. 'About 10 trillion won' betting on 'just one company' is plausible as the single-stock (not combined) figure, but I could not isolate a per-stock peak AUM number to confirm exactly.

claim: Microsoft, Google, Amazon and Meta spent $376 billion on AI infrastructure in 2025
quote: spent $376 billion on AI infrastructure in 2025
evidence: 2026 tech-press roundups put the same four companies' actual 2025 capex at $388-410B combined (Tom's Hardware, citing analysts); summing each company's own reported 2025 capex from a separate compilation (Amazon $125B + Google $91B + Meta $72B + Microsoft $90B = $378B) lands almost exactly on $376B. Plausible — sits inside the documented range and matches one independent sum closely — but not pinned to a single primary figure exactly.

claim: In 2026, Microsoft, Google, Amazon and Meta are on track to spend $725 billion [on AI infrastructure] — three-quarters of a trillion dollars a year
quote: they're on track to spend 725 billion
evidence: Tom's Hardware (citing analyst estimates) and an independent compilation of each company's own 2026 guidance (Amazon $200B + Google $175-185B + Meta $115-135B + Microsoft $110-120B) both land on $725B combined for 2026, up ~77% from ~$410B in 2025. Confirmed.

claim: [The video's sponsor] DeleteMe has, per the creator's personal account, scanned thousands of listings, removed over 68 instances of the creator's info being sold, and saved an estimated 14.5 hours of manual removal work
quote: scanned thousands of listings and removed over 68 instances of someone selling my info
evidence: A sponsor's personal-account numbers about one individual's own data-removal history are not independently checkable.

claim: [Sponsor] DeleteMe was named the number one data removal service by Wirecutter
quote: named the number one data removal service by Wirecutter
evidence: A secondary reference describes NYT Wirecutter's 2025 write-up naming DeleteMe its best/top data-removal pick, consistent with the ad copy — but I could not load Wirecutter's own page directly, and a separate 2026 independent test (Security.org) ranks DeleteMe third, behind Incogni and Aura. This is sponsored content read verbatim by the creator (tier 4: the advertiser talking about itself), which caps the verdict at plausible regardless of what outside sources show.

claim: In late June 2026, chip stocks in the US started selling off because investors were nervous ahead of Micron's earnings — which is how [the video argues] the US popped Korea's bubble
quote: chip stocks in the US started selling off
evidence: A real pre-earnings chip selloff is confirmed (Micron -13% on a late-June Tuesday; Nasdaq chip names fell again ahead of Micron's report). But Forbes attributes that specific selloff partly to a warning about risky single-stock ETFs issued by South Korea's own Financial Supervisory Service — i.e. Korea's leverage story was already feeding back into the US chip trade, not purely the other way around. The video's one-directional 'the US popped Korea's bubble' framing understates that the causality ran both ways.

claim: Micron is America's biggest chip maker and a competitor to Samsung and SK Hynix
quote: That is America's biggest chip maker
evidence: Micron is the largest US-based memory/HBM chipmaker and genuinely competes with Samsung and SK Hynix — but 'America's biggest chip maker' unqualified doesn't hold: by market cap Micron (~$1.05-1.2T, Sept 2026) is roughly a third of Nvidia's, which is the biggest US chipmaker by a wide margin. True for memory, not for chipmakers generally.

claim: In one session the KOSPI dropped something like 4.6%, and a week later Samsung and SK Hynix both went down more than 9% in one day
quote: the KOSPI dropped something like 4.6%
evidence: Single-day KOSPI/Samsung/SK Hynix drops of this size are well documented through the crash window (e.g. KOSPI -8.95% on 13 Jul, and double-digit down days for the two chipmakers later in July) — the specific 4.6% session and the following >9% day a week later weren't pinned to exact dates in the sources found, but sit inside the documented range and pattern of escalating single-day moves that period.

claim: 'Black Tuesday' — the KOSPI went down more than 10% in a day, one of the worst drops in the history of the Korean stock market
quote: Koreans are now calling Black Tuesday, which is where the KOSPI went down more than 10% in just a day
evidence: 'Black Tuesday' is the name multiple outlets (TheStreet, AFP) use for a KOSPI session that closed down 10.84%, with Samsung -13.39% and SK Hynix -14.65% the same day. Matches closely.

claim: A 10% one-day drop in the US stock market would be the third worst day in American history, only behind 1987 and the Great Depression
quote: that would be the third worst day in American history, only behind 1987 and the Great Depression
evidence: The ranking only works if you skip 2020: Black Monday 1987 (-22.6%) and the two worst Depression-era days (28 Oct 1929 -12.8%, 29 Oct 1929 -11.7%) are indeed worse than -10% — but so is the COVID crash of 16 Mar 2020 (-12.9%), which the claim omits entirely. Properly ranked, a 10% day would sit closer to 5th-6th worst, not 3rd.

claim: Under normal conditions about 2% of Korean margin accounts get force liquidated; during this crash that number went higher than 10%, about five times the normal rate
quote: about 2% of Korean margin accounts get force liquidated ... that number went higher than 10%
evidence: Matches closely: the forced-liquidation rate on short-term-loan stock purchases 'surged above 10%... compared to an average of just 2.1% over the prior six months' — roughly 5x, as claimed.

claim: Over the next two days [after Black Tuesday], more than 600 billion dollars got erased from Asian markets, and Japan went down more than 4%
quote: more than 600 billion dollars got erased from Asian markets
evidence: Searched three angles for a ~$600B/2-day, Japan -4% Asian selloff tied to the Korea margin-call crash. Found a comparably-sized regional rout (~$553B in two days, Japan -4%+, KOSPI -12.1% 'eclipsing 9/11') in the same general window, but it's attributed by that reporting to a later Iran/Strait-of-Hormuz shock, not the Korea AI-bubble crash the video describes. Couldn't confirm this is the same event rather than a conflation of two separate Asian sell-offs.

claim: As of June 2026, US margin debt hit roughly 4.5% of GDP — the highest level ever recorded, higher than the dot-com bubble, 2007, and the 2021 meme-stock bubble
quote: US margin debt just hit roughly 4 and 1/2% of GDP
evidence: A FINRA-sourced series puts margin-debt/GDP at 4.36% (Jul 2026) with a record high of 4.63%; a second write-up puts the figure at ~4.5%, explicitly 'surpassing the previous peaks before the dot-com bust, the 2008 financial crisis, and the 2021 meme-stock bubble.' Matches closely.

claim: Every time US margin debt went to an extreme — June 1968, December 1972, August 1987, March 2000, July 2007, January 2018, August 2021 — a crash or correction happened almost right after
quote: in June 1968, that was right before the market lost a third of its value
evidence: The general pattern is real and covered by financial-research sources: margin-debt/GDP peaked ahead of 1987 (~0.9%), 2000 (~2.6-3.0%), 2007 (~2.5%) and 2021 (3.97%), each followed by a major drawdown — a widely-circulated margin-debt chart (also citing June 1968 and Aug 1987) flags the same tops. I could not independently confirm the Dec 1972 and Jan 2018 dates specifically, and the best reachable sources are tier 3-4, so this caps at plausible rather than confirmed.

claim: Official [US] margin debt data only tracks traditional margin loans at brokerage accounts — it doesn't include leveraged ETFs, options, portfolio margin, or private credit
quote: the official margin data only tracks one kind of borrowing, which is traditional margin loans at brokerage accounts
evidence: FINRA's own rule (4521(d)) defines the reported figure as broker-dealer margin-account debit balances specifically — by construction not a measure of leverage embedded in ETFs, options or private credit, which is the point a tier-3 analysis piece on 'ratios that mislead investors' makes explicitly. Consistent with the claim, though no single source enumerated this exact exclusion list.

claim: Jim Chanos said the returns on AI spending are already going down — from 40% as a group a year and a half ago to about 20% today, and heading toward 10%
quote: it's gone from as a group 40% a year and a half ago to about 20% today
evidence: Matches a documented Chanos analysis closely: hyperscalers' (Google, Meta, Amazon, Microsoft, Oracle) incremental return on invested capital roughly halved from ~40% eighteen months ago to ~20% now, headed toward 10% if capex doesn't slow.

claim: OpenAI and Anthropic still lose tens of billions of dollars a year
quote: they still lose tens of billions of dollars a year
evidence: OpenAI alone is reported on track for ~$14B in 2026 losses (up from ~$8B in 2025) — consistent with 'tens of billions... a year' if read generously or as the pair's combined burn. Anthropic's own 2026 trajectory is toward its first operating profit, so 'tens of billions' fits OpenAI specifically better than it fits 'OpenAI and Anthropic' as a pair.

claim: OpenAI and Anthropic make up 70 to 80% of all the AI compute demand
quote: they make up 70 to 80% of all the AI compute demand
evidence: One widely-cited estimate (an individual industry commentator, tier 4) puts OpenAI+Anthropic at 70% of AI GPU capacity and 85% of AI compute spend today — matching the claim's range. But Epoch AI, a more rigorous research source, frames ~80% as where their compute share is headed over the next five years, not where it already stands — so the present-tense claim is only as strong as its weakest (tier-4) source.

claim: In 2026, IPOs have come to market at over 12% of GDP in post-IPO market cap — more than double the previous record, the dot-com bubble peak of 5%
quote: IPOs have come to market at over 12% of GDP in post-IPO market cap
evidence: Searched IPO-proceeds/GDP, post-IPO-market-cap/GDP, and Buffett-indicator variants three separate ways; no source states this specific 12%-of-GDP / 5%-dot-com-peak metric. JPMorgan's own read of the 2026 IPO wave calls it historic in dollar terms but modest relative to the market (~1% of S&P 500 market cap) — which cuts against the bubble framing here rather than supporting it. This is a load-bearing pillar of the video's US-bubble case and I could not source it after three follow-ups.

claim: In 2000, Coca-Cola needed 10,000 routers from Cisco; by 2001 they needed only 2,000 — Cisco's earnings collapsed and the NASDAQ went down 78%
quote: Coca-Cola needed 10,000 routers from Cisco. By 2001, they needed only 2,000
evidence: The NASDAQ's ~78% peak-to-trough dot-com decline and Cisco's collapse from its ~$500B/$80-a-share peak are well documented. The specific Coca-Cola '10,000 routers to 2,000' anecdote returns nothing across Cisco's SEC filings, its 2000-2001 earnings releases, and general dot-com retrospectives, despite the era being well within the searchable/SEC-archived record. Possibly a compressed or misattributed version of a real capex-cut story; can't confirm or debunk the specific numbers.

claim: Jim Chanos thinks the AI-spending reckoning could arrive sometime in late 2026 or 2027
quote: sometime in late 2026 or 2027
evidence: Prediction, not rated. Note: the attribution itself checks out — the same source that confirms Chanos's ROIC figures (claim 31) has him expecting this 'moment of reckoning' to emerge 'as early as between late 2026 and 2027,' matching the quote closely.

claim: After the Titanic hit the iceberg and was already sinking, the vice president of the company that owned it said, 'We have absolute confidence in the Titanic. We believe the boat is unsinkable'
quote: We have absolute confidence in the Titanic. We believe the boat is unsinkable
evidence: Philip Franklin, VP of the Titanic's owner (International Mercantile Marine/White Star Line), is recorded saying 'We place absolute confidence in the Titanic. We believe that the boat is unsinkable' — a near-verbatim match. One nuance: he said this around 10:30pm on 15 April 1912, roughly 20 hours after the Titanic had already fully sunk (2:20am that day), not in the first moments after striking the iceberg — so 'already sinking' understates how much had already happened by the time he said it, though the claim's literal wording still holds.

claim: Jim Chanos is the guy who called Enron
quote: Jim Chanos, the guy who called Enron
evidence: Widely documented: Chanos's short bet against Enron, initiated in late 2000, is credited as one of the most famous short calls in financial history ('the market call of the decade, if not the past fifty years' — Barron's, per MoneyWeek).

claim: At one point [during the crash], the only thing that stopped the KOSPI from going down even more was that the market was closed for a national holiday
quote: the only thing that stopped the Kospi from going down even more was that the market was literally closed for a national holiday
evidence: Searched for a national-holiday market closure during the crash window; results covered the same July 2026 plunge (circuit breakers, a ~23-34% peak-to-trough fall) in detail but none mentioned a holiday closure specifically, so I can't confirm or rule out this detail.

claim: [South Korea's] president, who held the emergency intervention, was the same person who had spent a year encouraging people to get into the stock market
quote: was the same person who spent a year encouraging people to get into the stock market
